sum: BASF sharpened its portfolio strategy during the week of November 23-27, 2026. On November 20, the chemicals group and cylib signed an agreement for the sale of BASF's Battery Recycling business, according to a BASF news release published on November 23.

The transaction covers BASF's battery recycling activities in Europe and North America, including intellectual property, customer contracts and partner relationships. It also includes the Black Mass production plant and the battery recycling prototype plant in Schwarzheide, Germany. Completion is expected between the second and third quarters of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions.

BASF said its Battery Materials division will focus exclusively on Cathode Active Materials, where it sees the strongest potential for customer value, differentiation and profitable development. The company will continue managing the recycling business until the transaction closes.

At its Capital Markets Day on November 24, BASF presented CoreShift, a program targeting up to 20 percent lower net cash fixed costs in its core businesses by 2029 compared with 2024. The plan spans eleven cross-divisional projects focused on portfolio scope, process harmonization, systems and organizational flexibility.

BASF also said Agricultural Solutions is progressing toward IPO readiness by mid-2027. The company said no decision has yet been made on the execution or timing of an IPO, which will depend in part on capital-market conditions. The division presented a gross peak-sales potential of around 15 billion euros from launches over the next 15 years.

items.t: BASF withdraws bid to acquire Evonik
sum: German chemical giant BASF has withdrawn its bid to acquire speciality chemicals company Evonik.

In a statement on its website on 19 November, BASF said its decision followed Evonik’s rejection of two non-binding offers, including a €24 (US$26.28)/share proposal which valued the company at approximately US$12.3bn.
BASF said despite its indication that it was prepared to consider a further moderate increase to its offer, Evonik’s executive board had remained unwilling to engage.
An assessment of Evonik’s prospects as an independent company and the associated risks did not justify further increases to its offer, BASF added.

Despite withdrawing its offer, Dr Markus Kamieth, chairman of BASF’s board of executive directors, said: “We continue to believe that the combination would create a more powerful chemical company under BASF’s ownership.”
Following BASF’s withdrawal of its bid, a 19 November Reuters report quoted Evonik’s interim CEO Claus Rettig as saying the company would now focus on its independent growth strategy.
BASF first approached Evonik in September and later raised its ‌offer to €11.2bn (US$12.3bn) after Evonik had rejected its initial proposal, Reuters wrote.

sum: BASF is stepping up its transformation drive, sharpening its business portfolio, cutting costs and preparing its Agricultural Solutions division for a potential stock market debut as it pushes ahead with its Winning Ways strategy.

At its Capital Markets Day in Ludwigshafen, Germany, on November 24, the chemical giant outlined progress on its restructuring agenda, unveiled an ambitious cost-reduction programme and reaffirmed its commitment to disciplined capital allocation and shareholder returns.

The company is now turning its attention to making its core businesses leaner, faster and more competitive through its newly launched CoreShift programme, which targets a reduction of up to 20% in net cash fixed costs by 2029 compared with 2024.

“We are delivering on our Winning Ways strategy. We have sharpened our portfolio and increased earnings power. Now we are taking the next step and are strengthening our core businesses with the CoreShift program so that they become simpler to run, faster to act, more competitive in costs and stronger to grow,” said Markus Kamieth, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors of BASF SE.
BASF has made significant progress in reshaping its portfolio, with several major transactions and business realignments completed or advancing.

A key milestone came in June 2026 with the completion of the Coatings transaction with Carlyle. The deal carried an enterprise value of €7.7 billion and generated a pre-tax disposal gain of €3.9 billion. BASF retains a 40% stake in Surventis, allowing it to participate in future growth.

Its Environmental Catalyst and Metal Solutions business, meanwhile, has been established as a standalone operation and rebranded as Metivo in September 2026. The business remains on track to deliver its target of €4 billion in cumulative cash flow between 2024 and 2030.

sum: BASF shares shed 2.6% on Friday to close at €49.45, caught in a downswing across German chemical equities that dpa-AFX linked to soft US market leads and a wave of analyst downgrades — most notably at Lanxess and Evonik. The retreat came barely a day after the Ludwigshafen group walked away from its pursuit of Evonik, a decision that had initially been greeted warmly: Reuters reported the stock climbed as much as 2.8% in the immediate aftermath of the withdrawal.

The takeover saga ended on Thursday, when BASF pulled the plug after Evonik turned down two unsolicited all-cash proposals. Its final offer stood at €24 per Evonik share. BASF argued that a richer price could not be justified given Evonik's standalone business prospects and the risks attached to them.

Sentiment on Friday was never going to be helped by Jefferies, which had cut BASF from "Hold" to "Underperform" on 11 November while keeping its €44 price target unchanged. Analyst Priyanka Patel pointed to eroding margins, excess capacity and higher gas prices, adding that demand has yet to show any meaningful recovery.

Away from the Evonik question, BASF has been reshaping its portfolio. On 12 November it signed an agreement to sell its global mining solutions business to SNF. The package includes a production site in Cork, Ireland, and roughly 140 employees. BASF expects the transaction to close in 2027, subject to merger clearance from the relevant authorities and the usual conditions being met.

At the same time, the company is adding bulk in Louisiana. BASF officially commissioned its new MDI plant in Geismar on 11 November, a project carrying a total investment of around $1 billion. The site's annual production capacity now stands at roughly 600,000 tonnes.

Further out, BASF Agricultural Solutions is targeting launches of its soybean resistance technology Nemasphere in the US and Brazil from 2028. On 16 November the company put the peak sales potential at more than €300 million. An EU import approval, according to BASF, completes the permits currently required across key export markets.

sum: BASF SE operates as a chemical company worldwide. It operates through six segments: Chemicals, Materials, Industrial Solutions, Surface Technologies, Nutrition & Care, and Agricultural Solutions. The Chemicals segment provides petrochemicals and intermediates. The Materials segment offers advanced materials and their precursors for applications and systems comprising isocyanates, polyamides, and inorganic basic products, as well as specialties for the plastics and plastics processing industries. The Industrial Solutions segment develops and markets ingredients and additives for industrial applications, such as polymer dispersions, resins, additives, chemical and refining catalysts, electronic materials, and antioxidants for automotive, petrochemical and petroleum processing, plastics and electronics, construction, electronics, paper coatings, and energy and resources industries. The Surface Technologies segment provides catalysts, battery materials, automotive OEM and refinish coatings, surface treatment, and precious and base metal services for the automotive and chemical industries. The Nutrition & Care segment offers ingredients for consumer applications in the areas of nutrition, home, and personal care applications; and serves the food and feed producers, pharmaceutical, cosmetics, detergents, and cleaner industries, as well as the consumer goods sector. The Agricultural Solutions segment provides seeds and traits, and seed treatment products; fungicides, herbicides, insecticides, and biological crop protection products; and digital solutions. The company engages in engineering and other; rental and leasing; and renewable energy trading, commodity trading activities. BASF SE was founded in 1865 and is headquartered in Ludwigshafen am Rhein, Germany.

sum: BASF has spent the past week stacking up announcements — a fresh US distribution alliance, a billion-dollar chemical plant coming online, and a soy seed technology with blockbuster ambitions. The market's response, so far, has been a shrug. Jefferies left its "Underperform" rating and 44 euro price target untouched yesterday, a stance that sits below the stock's current 50.06 euro level and signals that the broker wants proof of margin improvement, not just headlines about capacity and partnerships.

The timing is telling. The confirmation came on the heels of BASF's decision to walk away from its pursuit of Evonik after the company rejected its unsolicited all-cash offers. Jefferies's analyst had seen strategic merit in a deal but flagged execution risk around synergies; with the bid abandoned, both the potential upside and the synergy risk evaporate together. The unchanged rating makes clear the retreat gave the broker no reason to warm up to the shares.

On the operational front, BASF Corporation agreed a non-exclusive distribution cooperation with IMCD covering selected products from its industrial formulations portfolio in the United States. The arrangement opens an additional route to market — nothing more, nothing less. What matters for the equity story is whether IMCD reaches customers BASF's existing channels could not, or simply shifts volumes from one partner to another. In the latter case, the growth benefit would be thin.

That distinction — between a door opened and revenue actually booked — runs through every one of BASF's current initiatives. The clearest example sits in Louisiana, where the company started up a new MDI plant at its Geismar integrated site on November 11. The total investment came to roughly USD 1 billion, and annual production capacity at the site is set to nearly double to around 600,000 tonnes. The facility is running; whether that capacity gets utilized is an entirely separate question.

Here is where the margin test bites. A higher utilization rate on its own would not prove anything about profitability — what counts is whether the additional volumes sell at prices that lift the operating result.

sum: BASF's stock is trading squarely between two sharply divergent broker targets, and the gap says as much about the failed Evonik takeover as it does about the chemicals giant itself. Jefferies has reiterated its 44-euro target, implying further downside, while Bernstein is holding at 59 euros — a spread that leaves the current 50.73-euro price almost exactly in the middle.

The two houses agree on the facts of the abandoned deal but read them in opposite directions. BASF walked away from its pursuit of Evonik after the Essen-based specialty chemicals group rejected two non-binding all-cash offers, the last pitched at 24 euros per Evonik share. BASF had signalled a further moderate increase was possible but concluded that Evonik's standalone business outlook — and the risks attached to it — did not justify paying more.

For Jefferies analyst Priyanka Patel, the retreat validates her cautious stance. A combination would have carried strategic merit, she concedes, but BASF's heavy exposure to Europe and the danger of failing to deliver the promised synergies made the acquisition less appealing for the group. She keeps her underperform-equivalent view and the 44-euro target unchanged.
Management framed the decision as a matter of capital discipline, pointing to its attractive distribution policy. No additional payout was announced alongside the withdrawal.

Bernstein's James Hooper takes the other side of the argument, holding his 59-euro target. He does not rule out that Evonik's steep share-price slide following the rejection could shift the mood among its shareholders, who might press the supervisory board to reopen talks with BASF. That remains a scenario rather than a resumption of negotiations. The RAG-Stiftung, Evonik's anchor shareholder, did not back the transaction, according to the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung.

Evonik interim chief Claus Rettig, meanwhile, has doubled down on independence, saying the company intends to lift its value under its own steam and to play an active role in industry consolidation itself.
The collapse followed mounting opposition. Hendrik Wüst, premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, came out against the takeover yesterday.

sum: BASF is leaning on politicians and the RAG-Stiftung to unlock a fresh attempt at Evonik, but the draft concessions now circulating in Düsseldorf and Essen may not carry enough new money to move the needle. Reuters and Bloomberg reported that the chemicals group is sounding out state officials in North Rhine-Westphalia and Evonik's largest shareholder over extra job and site commitments, with a sweetened offer potentially landing within days at a price that remains undisclosed.

The gap between what BASF is offering and what sceptics want comes down to additionality. According to Reuters, BASF sketched out possible pledges on sites, jobs and apprenticeships in a letter to the state government and the RAG-Stiftung — but the document still carries placeholders where timeframes and investment sums should sit. Bloomberg's account goes further, suggesting BASF could rule out compulsory redundancies for a period still to be negotiated, keep every German production site, and add spending on research and development plus the low-carbon conversion of its plants.

Much of that ground has been covered before. The Handelsblatt, citing a draft dated 11 November, reported plans to roll over existing employee commitments and keep the Marl and Wesseling chemical parks running, with Essen retained as a group location hosting a board division responsible for more than EUR 10 billion in revenue. Back in late October, BASF had already promised to take on Evonik's employment guarantees through 2032 and to keep Marl and Wesseling operating with roughly 3,500 jobs.

That history is precisely the problem. Insiders quoted by the Handelsblatt see little material substance beyond what has already been pledged, and Evonik works council representative Hussin El Moussaoui made the same point — restating the status quo creates no added value. Repeating known guarantees, in other words, looks unlikely to dislodge the reservations on the labour side.

For BASF, the trade-off is becoming explicit. Deeper commitments may smooth the path to approval, yet employment and site guarantees can blunt the savings that job cuts or consolidation would otherwise deliver — and that in turn caps the takeover price the company can economically justify.

sum: BASF has returned roughly 591,000 of its own shares to the treasury in a single week, the company disclosed, while simultaneously firing up a new MDI production train in Louisiana and pushing a nematode-resistant soybean trait toward commercialization. The three announcements land against a less flattering backdrop: Jefferies cut the chemical maker to "Underperform" on November 11, with analyst Priyanka Patel flagging shrinking margins, persistent overcapacity, elevated gas prices and a demand recovery that has yet to materialize.
The buyback, executed between November 9 and November 13, brought cumulative repurchases under the program to about 8.54 million shares. BASF stock shed 1.2% in the prior session.

At the Geismar complex in Louisiana, BASF officially commissioned its new MDI plant on November 11. The investment totaled roughly USD 1 billion and lifts annual MDI capacity at the site to about 600,000 metric tons. Unlike the soybean trait, this is hardware already running — a completed capital project rather than a promise.

The distinction matters for how investors weigh the news flow. Additional capacity and an expanded product slate create options; they do not by themselves translate into earnings. Nor does the buyback answer that operational question, since it changes the share count rather than the profit pool.

BASF Agricultural Solutions, meanwhile, is advancing Nemasphere, a soybean trait designed to resist nematodes. Management pegs peak sales potential at more than EUR 300 million, with launches in the U.S. and Brazil slated for 2028. According to the company, the latest EU import approval completes the clearances currently required in key export markets.

That timeline sits years out, so the trait belongs in a different bucket from Geismar: one is a finished investment, the other a long-dated product prospect. Both feed into the investment case, but neither substitutes for proof of extra operating profit.

Closer on the calendar is a planned switch in the European business. From January 2027, BASF intends to run its polyisobutene portfolio for external customers entirely on renewable electricity. That is a more tangible execution step than the 2028 seed launches, though it is no guarantee of higher earnings either.

sum: The stock’s recent trajectory has been notably weak, with BASF India Ltd trading below all key moving averages — the 5-day, 20-day, 50-day, 100-day, and 200-day — signalling sustained downward momentum. This is in stark contrast to the Sensex, which has gained 10.45% over the last three weeks and continues to climb, supported by mega-cap stocks. The index closed at 82,238.05, up 0.79% on the day, reflecting broad market optimism that has not extended to this specialty chemicals company. What is driving such persistent weakness in BASF India Ltd when the broader market is in rally mode?

Despite the share price decline, the company’s recent quarterly results present a complex narrative. The profit after tax (PAT) for the quarter ending September 2026 fell sharply by 39.7% to Rs 61.71 crores, while PBDIT hit a low of Rs 91.48 crores. Operating profit to net sales ratio also dropped to a concerning 1.89%, the lowest in recent quarters. These figures highlight near-term pressures on profitability, which have likely contributed to the negative sentiment.

However, over the past year, BASF India Ltd has recorded a 51.1% increase in profits, a notable improvement that contrasts with the share price performance. This disconnect between earnings growth and stock price decline raises questions about market confidence in the sustainability of these gains. Could the market be discounting risks not immediately visible in the headline profit numbers?

Over the last five years, the company’s operating profit has declined at an annual rate of -1.93%, reflecting challenges in sustaining growth. sum: BASF's October analyst scorecard lands on the friendly side: twelve of 19 ratings carry a Buy call, against five Holds and two Sells. Yet the same consensus that leans positive offers little in the way of upside, with the average price target sitting at EUR 54.08.

That gap between recommendation and expectation is the story. A Friday close of EUR 53.30 already puts the stock within touching distance of the mean target, so the bullish majority on its own is no argument for a big remaining re-rating.

Individual targets published in October run from EUR 40 to EUR 61, a range that shows how far apart analysts stand on what the shares are actually worth. The average smooths those differences without resolving them, which means the headline count of Buy ratings tells only half the tale. What matters just as much is the valuation scenario sitting behind each call.

Recent revisions illustrate the point. Deutsche Bank Research cut BASF to Hold from Buy on Monday, trimming its target to EUR 53 from EUR 60, citing greater complexity, execution risk and a heavier concentration on Europe. Bernstein Research moved the other way on conviction, keeping its Outperform rating on Thursday while shaving its target to EUR 59 from EUR 61.

Behind the caution lies BASF's approach to Evonik. According to media reports, BASF is offering EUR 24 per share, valuing Evonik's equity at roughly EUR 11.2 billion — a premium of about 39% to the price before takeover interest became public.

Evonik reviewed BASF's letter and declined to enter negotiations on that basis, though it left the door open to a confidential exchange of information only. Formal talks have not begun, and Reuters reported that BASF met the refusal with incomprehension. Chief executive Markus Kamieth had stressed on Wednesday that BASF would not overpay for Evonik, saying any transaction would go ahead only if it created value for BASF shareholders.

For BASF investors, the two threads stay separate: analysts lean positive on the stock, while the fate of the takeover push remains unresolved. Nothing in the published targets amounts to a verdict on a possible deal.

sum: The Tamarac city commission on Wednesday will discuss how to allocate $315,195.02 in funds the city received as its net share of a national class action settlement over contamination of public water systems with PFAS, a group of synthetic “forever chemicals.”

items.t: The Precedent : Federal Circuit Affirms Antitrust Liability for Patent Tying in Ingevity Corp. v. BASF Corp
sum: In this edition of The Precedent, we outline the decision in Ingevity Corp. v. BASF Corp.

In Ingevity Corp. v. BASF Corp., the Federal Circuit affirmed a jury verdict finding that Ingevity Corp. (Ingevity) violated antitrust laws by tying licenses to its fuel‑vapor canister patent to purchases of its unpatented carbon honeycombs. The Federal Circuit upheld a trebled damages award totaling more than $84 million and rejected Ingevity’s arguments that its honeycombs were not staple goods — which would have permitted Ingevity to control the honeycombs — that its conduct was immune from antitrust laws because it has the ability to enforce its patents and that the award must be vacated because BASF Corp. (BASF) failed to disaggregate damages.

- Did BASF present sufficient evidence for the jury to find that Ingevity’s carbon honeycombs were staple goods with substantial non‑infringing uses, which would defeat Ingevity’s patent misuse defense?
- Was Ingevity’s conduct immune from antitrust liability because Ingevity’s actions involved patent enforcement activity and communications about patent rights?
- Was the jury’s antitrust damages award, including its treatment of causation and apportionment, supported by the record?
- Substantial evidence supported the jury’s finding that Ingevity’s honeycombs were staple goods that could be used in non‑infringing applications, which defeated Ingevity’s patent misuse defense.
- Ingevity had waived its immunity argument by failing to raise it before the trial court. The trial court did not commit any plain error that warranted relief.

Parkinson’s risk increases with exposure to common chemical, study suggests
sum: A pesticide commonly used in America’s food supply has been linked to Parkinson’s disease, new research suggests.
A UCLA study published in the journal Springer Nature Link suggests that exposure to chlorpyrifos could increase the risk of the neurological disease.
The chemical is often used on agricultural products like soybeans, fruit and nut trees, broccoli, cauliflower and other row crops, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.
The study compared 829 people with Parkinson’s to 824 people without the disease over a 45-year period, focusing on their proximity to chlorpyrifos.
The researchers also conducted mouse experiments, where mice inhaled the pesticide as humans would for 11 weeks. Experiments were also carried out on zebrafish to study cell-level brain damage.
In humans, the study revealed that long-term exposure to chlorpyrifos led to more than a 2.5 times higher risk of Parkinson’s.
In mice, exposure to the pesticide caused movement problems similar to Parkinson’s symptoms, loss of dopamine-producing neurons, increased brain inflammation and build-up of harmful proteins.

sum: The chemicals giant finds itself at an unusual crossroads: its stock is trading within striking distance of a yearly high, yet the analyst community is growing noticeably cooler on the shares. Two separate research houses — MWB among them — trimmed their recommendations on BASF from "Buy" to "Hold" on Wednesday, citing a familiar refrain: the valuation gap to fair value has closed, and a fresh catalyst has yet to emerge. Price targets remain pinned at €55.00.

The market's response was telling. Rather than punishing the stock for the downgrades, BASF shares edged up 1.3% to €53.45, leaving the paper just 2.9% shy of its 52-week high of €55.05. That resilience speaks to the structural supports underpinning the stock — cost savings programs and an ongoing share buyback — even as the free cash flow conversion continues to draw criticism from the sell-side.

MWB framed its decision around a "normalized risk-reward profile," suggesting the asymmetry that once favored upside has flattened after months of strong price appreciation. The implication for investors is straightforward: the tailwind from obvious undervaluation has largely played out, and further gains will now require concrete operational triggers rather than a simple re-rating.

Operationally, the picture is more complicated. BASF was forced to postpone the planned commissioning of a facility at its Industriepark Lausitz site in Schwarzheide on Wednesday after an attack on a substation near Jänschwalde disrupted regional power supplies. The site, part of the group's battery materials operations, sits within the 300-hectare industrial park. No new start-up date has been announced.

The delay is an unwelcome wrinkle for a division that forms part of BASF's strategic growth ambitions in the energy transition space, though it appears to be an external disruption rather than a reflection of any internal execution issues.

Meanwhile, the planned carve-out of BASF's agricultural chemicals division is gathering pace. Board member Livio Tedeschi confirmed last Wednesday that the separation of the business in North and South America and Europe is now largely complete, with Asia expected to follow by year-end.

sum: KUALA LUMPUR (Dec 4): APB Resources Bhd (KL:APB) said its wholly owned subsidiary has filed a claim with an arbitral tribunal against BASF PETRONAS Chemicals Sdn Bhd for alleged unpaid contract sums and payment for additional works.

In a filing with Bursa Malaysia on Thursday, APB said Amalgamated Metal Corporation (M) Sdn Bhd (AMC) is seeking payment for a remaining sum of €1.85 million (RM8.82 million) under a 2017 contract, as well as €439,482 (RM2.10 million) for additional works carried out for a steam boiler and turbine package project.

Under the contract, AMC was the on-shore consortium partner while Christof Projects GmbH was the off-shore consortium partner appointed by BASF PETRONAS Chemicals, a Malaysia-based joint venture between BASF and Petroliam Nasional Bhd (PETRONAS), for supply, installation, and commissioning works.

According to APB, AMC had completed its scope of works for the project in May 2019 and invoiced BASF PETRONAS Chemicals in accordance with the agreed payment procedures, but the company “failed, neglected and/or refused” to make the remaining payments.

The filing of the statement of claim follows a notice of arbitration by AMC and an unsuccessful jurisdictional challenge by BASF PETRONAS Chemicals before the tribunal. Following the dismissal, BASF PETRONAS Chemicals subsequently sought to set aside the tribunal's decision through an application at the High Court of Singapore.

"In accordance with the directions given by the tribunal, AMC has now served the statement of claim on BASF PETRONAS Chemicals to formally commence the substantive arbitral process while awaiting the outcome of Singapore High Court proceedings," APB said. "AMC will continue to pursue its rights and remedies under the contract."

APB said the financial impact of the arbitration is subject to the final outcome of the proceedings, noting that the amount claimed had been fully impaired in the previous financial year and may be reversed in the event of a successful recovery.
